title: Andrew Ross Sorkin Doubts OpenAI Will Be “Worth More Than Anthropic.” That’s a Problem for Microsoft - TIKR.com
content: Anthropic (ANT) priced its IPO at $83 a share and opened at $111.50 on Thursday. On CNBC’s Power Lunch that day, Andrew Ross Sorkin said: “I’d be shocked if and when OpenAI goes public that they are worth more than Anthropic.” His reasoning: “Anthropic has been maniacally focused on the enterprise and they have found customers willing to pay and pay an extraordinary premium with an extraordinary margin.” That’s an awkward ranking for Microsoft (MSFT), whose biggest AI lab bet is OpenAI. Amazon (AMZN) backed Anthropic instead, and Oracle (ORCL) has even more riding on OpenAI than Microsoft does. When OpenAI restructured in October 2025, Microsoft valued its stake at about $135 billion, roughly 27% of the company. Microsoft’s cloud business also leans on OpenAI, which made up about 45% of Microsoft’s $625 billion commercial backlog at the end of 2025. The stake already moves Microsoft’s earnings. It added a $6.5 billion pre-tax gain in fiscal 2026 (the year to June 2026), after a $4.8 billion loss the year before, as net income climbed to $133.7 billion: Amazon sits on the other side: Anthropic’s amended S-1 showed it holding 48.2% of Anthropic’s outstanding class N stock. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Anthropic’s Analyst Ratings Anthropic marketed its IPO at a valuation of up to about $1.4 trillion, and its shares gave back most of their opening gain by Friday morning. OpenAI, meanwhile, reportedly cut its own fundraising target to $1.25 trillion from $1.4 trillion in October. At Microsoft’s roughly 27%, every $100 billion that comes off OpenAI’s price takes about $27 billion off the stake. Anthropic isn’t a flawless yardstick either: TIKR puts its gross margin over the last 12 months at 22.3%. If its price keeps sliding, OpenAI gets measured against an even lower bar. Microsoft also owns a piece of Anthropic. It agreed in November 2025 to invest up to $5 billion and booked a $3.2 billion gain on the stake in the June quarter, and Anthropic committed to buy $30 billion of Azure compute. But that’s small next to the OpenAI stake. Oracle has no such hedge. S&P has said OpenAI accounts for about half of Oracle’s $664 billion backlog, and Oracle’s free cash flow was negative $5 billion in the quarter to Aug. 31. If OpenAI can’t raise money at the price it wants, Oracle has the most to lose of the three. Analysts still expect Microsoft’s revenue to grow about 19% in fiscal 2027, to $396 billion, and another 21% in fiscal 2028: Azure drives much of that growth, and OpenAI is Azure’s biggest customer. A cheaper OpenAI wouldn’t dent this year’s revenue, but a lab that struggles to raise money will struggle to pay for its compute. The stock already prices in some doubt. Microsoft trades at 24x forward earnings, well below its five-year average of 29x: The way I see it, Sorkin is probably right, and Microsoft shareholders will feel it. Its OpenAI stake and the backlog behind it now get judged against Anthropic, and that should keep a lid on Microsoft’s multiple until OpenAI proves otherwise. Of course, OpenAI’s listing is expected next year, and its own numbers could flip the ranking. Until then, Anthropic’s first quarter as a public company and Microsoft’s next report, due in late January, are the best reads. title: Cramer: Microsoft the “Smartest of the Hyperscalers” With Relentless Focus on Positive Cashflow. That Includes Asking 60,000 Employees to Quit - TIKR.com
content: @Natee Meepian's Images via Canva, @Worawee Meepian's Images via Canva Microsoft (MSFT) offered buyouts to 60,000 employees in October, in place of another big round of layoffs. CEO Satya Nadella explained why at The New York Times DealBook Summit on Nov. 18, and a day later Jim Cramer posted what Nadella had told him about the money side: “Microsoft is determined to maintain positive operating cash flow. That’s what Satya tells me. Does that make it the smartest of the hyperscalers???” It’s a fair question. Amazon (AMZN), Meta Platforms (META) and Oracle (ORCL) all reported negative free cash flow in their latest quarters, as AI data center spending outran the cash their businesses brought in. Nadella didn’t pitch the buyouts as a cost cut. He told Andrew Ross Sorkin the offer was “to make sure that at least everyone felt like they had agency in making choices,” as Microsoft reorganizes so that every employee uses AI and manages it. Still, fewer people doing more of the work shows up in the cost line. In fiscal 2026 (the year to June), headcount fell 2% and operating expenses grew 7%, against 18% revenue growth. See the full breakdown of Buy, Hold, and Sell ratings on Microsoft, along with Wall Street’s revenue and earnings estimates, all in one place. More than 500,000 investors use TIKR to research stocks like this one. See Microsoft’s Analyst Ratings Microsoft brought in $58 billion of operating cash in the September quarter alone. Free cash flow is the harder bar, and management said in July it expects it to stay positive in fiscal 2027. Analysts agree, but they expect it to fall by more than half this fiscal year before it recovers: The September quarter brought in $18.6 billion of free cash flow, down 27% from a year earlier, so Microsoft needs about $13.4 billion more from the next three quarters combined to reach the $32.0 billion consensus. The drop comes from capex, which grew nearly 5x in four fiscal years while operating cash flow roughly doubled: In fiscal 2026 alone, capex rose $51.4 billion and operating cash flow rose $46.8 billion, so free cash flow fell for a second straight year. Amazon shows what happens once spending gets ahead of cash. This week, a poster on the r/ValueInvesting subreddit put Amazon’s owner earnings at plus $89 billion using depreciation as the cost of upkeep, and minus $47 billion counting all of its capex. TIKR’s figures back that up, with Amazon’s free cash flow negative for three straight quarters: Over the four quarters to Sept. 30, Amazon’s free cash flow added up to negative $46.9 billion. Microsoft’s entire operating expense line was $70.2 billion in fiscal 2026, against $115.9 billion of cash capex. Meta cut headcount 15% over the year to Sept. 30, and its free cash flow was still negative $2.12 billion in the September quarter, as $34.91 billion of capex, including finance-lease principal, topped its $32.79 billion of operating cash flow. Oracle sold $20 billion of stock through an at-the-market program in the quarter to Aug. 31, while its free cash flow was negative $5 billion. So the exits matter most for Microsoft’s operating margin, which management expects to fall by less than 1 point in fiscal 2027. Free cash flow is staying positive because of the business itself: operating cash flow rose 29% in the September quarter. On cash, Microsoft is the smartest of the hyperscalers right now. Still, the full bill is bigger than the cash line shows: free cash flow leaves out finance leases, which came to $7.4 billion in the September quarter alone. Microsoft reports its December quarter in late January, with capex guided above $50 billion. A year earlier, that quarter’s free cash flow was just $5.9 billion. Another positive quarter would put Microsoft well on its way to the $32.0 billion consensus, and a negative one would cast doubt on management’s call. At a Record High, the Upside Is Smaller. Microsoft ($MSFT) looks like a long over a two-year horizon, to late 2028, with a target of $650. That's about 17% above Wednesday's $555.80 close, a record high. Of the four big AI spenders, Microsoft is the only one still producing large free cash flow: about $60B over the past year, against −$47B at Amazon. Azure grew 48% last quarter, and management guides 49–50% for the next. The catch is the price. At about 25x 2027 earnings, Microsoft carries the highest multiple of the group, so the upside is smaller than the quality suggests. The starting point is a five-factor quant model built by the author (see the disclosure at the end). It grades Microsoft A, 4.26 out of 5, against the Technology sector, recalculated on November 1. Profitability scores 4.96 and momentum 4.08. Financial health scores B+. Two grades stand out. Growth is only C+, because Microsoft is ranked against chip and software companies growing faster. Valuation is D. The model also reads Microsoft as a wide-moat business, with returns above its cost of capital in nine of the last ten years. Revenue in the quarter to September was $92.3B, up 19%. Operating income rose 21%, and the operating margin held at about 50%. EPS was $4.89, up 18% excluding the impact of the OpenAI investment. For the December quarter, Microsoft guides revenue to $96.0–97.1B, growth of 18–19%. The growth is concentrated in the cloud. Microsoft Cloud revenue reached $63.9B, up 30%, with growth accelerating. Azure grew 48%, even though some third-party capacity deliveries slipped. Commercial remaining performance obligations, the contracted backlog, rose 73% to $677B. About 30% of that should turn into revenue within twelve months. Copilot is starting to show up in the numbers. Daily users rose nearly 50% from the prior quarter and more than fivefold from a year ago. The number of customers with more than 50,000 seats is up more than eightfold, and Volkswagen plans to roll Copilot out to over 330,000 employees. The weak spot is the PC. Windows OEM revenue fell 27% as the market digested last year's Windows 10 upgrade cycle and memory costs pushed up PC prices. Management guides Windows OEM and devices down in the mid-30s next quarter. Xbox revenue fell 2%. This is what separates Microsoft from the rest of the group. Over the past twelve months, Microsoft generated about $60B of free cash flow. Meta generated $28.7B and Alphabet $19.7B, while Amazon burned $46.9B. Microsoft spent 69% of its operating cash flow on capex, the lowest share of the four. As The Motley Fool noted this week, it is the only one of them forecasting positive free cash flow next year. Capex is still climbing fast. Cash paid for property and equipment was $39.4B in the quarter. Including $7.4B of finance leases, total capex was $45.2B. For calendar 2026, capex should come in around $170B, and the CFO expects more than $50B next quarter. Operating cash flow is keeping pace, though: it rose 29% to $58.0B. Free cash flow was $18.6B, and Microsoft returned $10.2B to shareholders through dividends and share repurchases. The balance sheet is in good shape, with $64.6B of cash and short-term investments against $35.5B of debt. Finance leases add another $98.5B. The CFO said Microsoft will "access additional sources of funding when we believe it is attractive to do so," and noted it has not yet tapped the debt markets. That stands in contrast to the equity and debt raises at its peers. Next to Alphabet, Amazon and Meta, Microsoft has the highest operating margin (47%), the lowest capex intensity (69% of operating cash flow), and revenue growth (19%) between Amazon's and Alphabet's. The market has noticed. At 25.2x 2027 earnings, Microsoft trades above Amazon (24.8x), Alphabet (19.1x) and Meta (18.5x). The author's own valuation models put median fair value near $288. These models are less distorted here than for the other three, because Microsoft's free cash flow is still large. The gap mostly reflects how much growth the current price already assumes. Consensus EPS for fiscal 2028 (ending June 2028) is $24.03. A 27x multiple on that gives about $650. That's roughly where Microsoft has traded over recent years, and it is above the Street's average target of $612 (range $440–$750). The target implies less upside than for the other AI spenders. The trade-off is a much stronger cash position while the build-out continues. On the positive side, Copilot revenue becoming large enough to report separately, or Azure holding near 50% into 2027, would raise the case for a higher multiple. Most ESG ratings tell you how well a company reports. Very few tell you whether the business is actually efficient. $MSFT is the cleanest example I know of the gap. It carries strong sustainability ratings and publishes one of the more thorough environmental reports in the market. It also disclosed in its 2026 report that total emissions across Scopes 1, 2 and 3 rose 25% year on year, driven by datacenter expansion. Its own figures run from 13 million tonnes of CO2 equivalent in 2020 to 20 million in 2025, against a pledge to be carbon negative by 2030. Energy use, by its own account, has grown far faster than revenue. None of that makes Microsoft a bad company. It is one of the best-run businesses in the world. It makes it a company where a sustainability rating and operational efficiency are answering two different questions. Back in 2021 we started checking what ESG funds actually held. A number held oil majors. Others held the technology companies building energy-hungry AI infrastructure. These were not obscure funds, and they carried strong ratings. Eco-efficiency asks how much energy and material a company consumes to earn each dollar of return. It draws on emissions, energy and resource intensity, reported operational data, and thermodynamic return on invested capital, which puts return against the energy and resources consumed to produce it. A business that needs less energy and material to earn a dollar is usually better run. It wastes less, it is less exposed when input costs move, and it has more room when conditions turn. That makes it a capital preservation measure rather than a moral one. Buying a stock because it carries a sustainability label, at any price, is not a plan. title: Tech Outages At Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) And Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL) Cast Shadow Over Mullin's Global Threat Testimony - Foreign Policy Journal
content: By David Prior | Nov 20, 2026 | Featured, News & Analysis, Politics A cascading wave of widespread technology failures at some of America’s largest companies has set an uneasy backdrop for high-stakes congressional oversight hearings in Washington. Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin is facing pointed questioning from lawmakers on Capitol Hill over the administration’s assessment of worldwide security threats. The timing of his appearance has drawn heightened scrutiny given the recent rash of major outages that disrupted services across Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT), Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL), and several major airline networks. Those failures have renewed urgent questions about the resilience of critical digital infrastructure and whether the country’s technology backbone is adequately protected against both accidental and deliberate disruption. Space Force chief software officer Nicolas Chaillan weighed in on the situation, offering his perspective on the wave of tech failures and what they signal about broader systemic vulnerabilities. Chaillan’s comments underline a growing concern among defense and security professionals that widespread outages, regardless of their origin, expose dangerous fragility in systems that underpin everyday life. Airline networks were among the most visible casualties of the disruptions, with passengers facing delays and service interruptions that rippled across the broader transportation sector. For Mullin, the outages represent an unavoidable talking point as he confronts legislators eager to probe whether the federal government has a credible plan to prevent or respond to large-scale infrastructure failures. The convergence of a global threat briefing with fresh evidence of domestic technological fragility is likely to shape the tone and focus of the committee’s line of questioning considerably. Capitol Hill hearings on national security have increasingly expanded their scope to include cyber resilience and the private sector’s role in safeguarding infrastructure that millions of Americans depend on daily. The Mullin testimony arrives at a moment when policymakers are under pressure to demonstrate that oversight mechanisms can keep pace with the speed and scale of modern technological disruption. Whether the recent outages were the result of technical failures, cyberattacks, or some combination of both remains a central question that lawmakers are expected to press Mullin to answer directly. "We have created enormous anxiety in people sort of feeling that they don't have control of their own destiny because [of] the way we have talked about this AI revolution." Nadella explained how Microsoft's evolving acceptance of AI influenced this decision. "Let's take software engineering. We went from, 'Well, we don't buy that AI can ever do software.' To now rediscovering that software engineering is very much alive and, in fact, is going to thrive, except the way the team is organized and the work that a software engineer does has now got a new operating point," Nadella told Sorkin. For some employees, "that reorganization and change is sort of hard, right?" said Nadella, who added that, in his opinion, "it has to be done." Nadella believes at some point, every employee that uses a computer will manage AI agents instead of doing the work themselves. "That level of direction is what, by the way, is going to happen in all jobs," he told Sorkin. But until then, the 60,000 Microsoft employees who were given voluntary buyouts have to make a decision on whether to accept the company's offer before the deadline in early December. Voluntary buyouts can reduce the need for — or size of — layoffs, which can be good for companies that want to avoid the stress and stigma of laying off swaths of workers. For employees, a voluntary buyout can provide several benefits. First, some employees may already be looking at their options and have considered leaving their current employer. Second, some employees who receive buyout offers might feel as if they won't have a difficult time finding a new position elsewhere. And third, employees who want to stay at the company may be less likely to be laid off in the future if enough of their colleagues take the buyout. title: $1 Million In Microsoft 10 Years Ago: Worth It? - Trefis
content: Today’s big story: Will 2027 Be A 2022 Repeat For Stocks? $1 million put into Microsoft at the Friday, Nov 18, 2016 close was worth about $9.25 million at Thursday’s close. That counts dividends put back into the stock. That is more than nine times the money. On price alone, the stake came to $8,256,835. The ride was harder than that end number suggests. Microsoft’s worst fall in the ten years was 37.6%. It ran from Nov 19, 2021 to Nov 3, 2022. Counting from the Nov 19, 2021 peak, the stock took 573 days to close above it again. Its most recent big fall, 34.9% to June 25, 2026, came close to that worst one. Is Microsoft the big tech stock best placed to ride out an AI slowdown? This article looks at the ride first. It asks how far Microsoft fell and how long it took to heal, against Nvidia and Amazon. The question is timely. Stocks fell broadly on Thursday. Microsoft closed down 2.0% at $498.30. Microsoft closed at $343.11 on Nov 19, 2021. It hit a low of $214.25 on Nov 3, 2022. The fall lasted 349 days, and the climb back took another 224 days. The stock first closed above its old peak on June 15, 2023, at $348.10. This article does not try to say what caused this fall or the others. Microsoft dropped 37.6% and needed 573 days from its peak to get back above it. If Microsoft is a big part of your savings, that is a long drop to sit through and a long wait just to get even. When the market has fallen, the Trefis High Quality (HQ) Portfolio has lost about 81 cents for every $1 its benchmark lost, on average. See the HQ record. That was not the only deep fall. Amazon took 1,008 days. Our read: Microsoft’s falls were shallower, but not always shorter. The QQQ fund fell 35.6% in the same slump, which began on Nov 19, 2021. That is a little less than Microsoft’s 37.6%. QQQ, like Microsoft, had four falls of 20% or more. Nvidia’s path was rougher. It had eight falls of 20% or more, and seven of them healed. The one still open began at its Oct 6, 2026 record close. Nvidia is 39.0% below that record. Amazon had five such falls, and all five healed. The company has detailed plans to add vast new capacity across its global network, a move that speaks directly to the question dominating the market this week: how quickly, and how durably, AI-infrastructure spending will keep scaling. For readers who follow Bluechip Stocks, Microsoft remains a closely watched name in the group. The expansion push builds on a stretch in which Microsoft's cloud arm has grown briskly, carried by enterprises moving workloads to Azure and by a wave of demand tied to generative-AI features woven across the company's software. Management has framed the added capacity as a response to that demand rather than a speculative bet, pointing to utilization across its data-center fleet as the reason more campuses are coming online. The backdrop into which this news landed has been unsettled. The artificial-intelligence trade is being tested after a sharp advance, semiconductor names have seesawed, and Federal Reserve meeting minutes have kept rate expectations in flux against a thin economic-data calendar. Sentiment has been choppy, and the market's front-running groups have rotated as traders reassess how much of the AI story is already priced in. Microsoft operates one of the broadest franchises in technology, spanning the Windows platform, the Office productivity suite, the Azure cloud, LinkedIn, the Dynamics business applications, security offerings and a gaming arm anchored by Xbox. That spread gives the company multiple engines of growth and a deep, recurring relationship with enterprises and consumers alike. Microsoft sits in a rare spot: it owns both the applications many organizations run every day and a growing share of the infrastructure those applications increasingly depend on. That dual position lets the company capture demand at several layers of the stack, from the software a worker touches to the servers humming in a distant data center, and it is the reason the name is treated as a core position within the broad market. The headline development is the scale of the capacity being added. Microsoft has outlined plans to expand its data-center fleet substantially, with new campuses designed around the power and cooling demands of dense AI computing. The build-out is a concrete expression of how the company expects demand to unfold, and it has become a focal point for a market trying to gauge the durability of the broader spending wave. Executing a build-out of this magnitude is an operational challenge in its own right. Sourcing components, securing power, constructing campuses on schedule and bringing capacity online efficiently all bear on how smoothly demand is met, and the market watches those details closely because they shape how quickly the company can convert surging interest into live services. The hyperscale race carries real challenges. Building at scale demands enormous capital, access to power and a steady supply of specialized chips, and any bottleneck in those inputs can slow the pace of expansion. Energy availability in particular has become a gating factor, with demand for electricity around data centers climbing even as grids strain to keep up. Microsoft competes with the other hyperscale cloud providers for enterprise workloads, with a wide field of software firms across productivity and business applications, and with a growing roster of AI specialists. What distinguishes its position is the way its software estate and its cloud infrastructure reinforce each other, so that demand for one tends to pull through demand for the other. Because of its size and its central role in the cloud and AI story, Microsoft functions as a barometer for enterprise technology spending as a whole. When the company signals that it is building capacity to meet demand, the market reads it as a vote of confidence in the durability of the AI transition, and that signal ripples across suppliers, power providers and the wider technology complex. Microsoft CEO Satya Nadella explained Wednesday why he offered buyouts to 60,000 of his employees in October, essentially urging them to voluntarily quit instead of reducing the workforce via another massive layoff. Short answer: AI, but not, he insists, in the way you might expect. He's not saying he's replacing employees with AI, especially software engineers. He's saying he's reorganizing Microsoft into a company where everyone uses AI to do their work, and their jobs become focused on managing that AI. The buyout was "to make sure that at least everyone felt like they had agency in making choices," he told Andrew Ross Sorkin during the DealBook Summit. "Let's take software engineering. We went from, 'Well, we don't buy that AI can ever do software.' To suddenly, 'Wow, it can do all software, and why do we need software engineers?' To now rediscovering that software engineering is very much alive and, in fact, is going to thrive, except the way the team is organized and the work that a software engineer does has now got a new operating point," he explained. For some people, "that reorganization and change is sort of hard, right?" he added, "but, I mean, it has to be done." He offered the example of the team that builds Cowork, the AI agent in Microsoft 365 apps. He said the team consists of just 11 developers who have mastered using AI to do their jobs. "They build a software factory that builds the product. They don't build the product." He believes that every employee will one day similarly become a manager of agents, rather than a person directly doing the work. "That level of direction is what, by the way, is going to happen in all jobs." But Microsoft, as a 51-year-old company, didn't grow up as an AI-first company. "So the question is, how quickly can an incumbent transform the work, the workflow, and the work artifact, and with all the wage support that goes with it?" he said. "It's going to take a bit more time than anyone expects. And there is going to be in all of this, you know, people who may say, 'Hey, I have some other choices I want to make.'" When asked about this same topic — why ask 60,000 people to voluntarily resign — last week by Gergely Orosz on his The Pragmatic Engineer podcast, Nadella further explained, "We have created enormous anxiety in people sort of feeling that they don't have control of their own destiny because the way we have talked about this AI revolution." He called out talk about the singularity (the hypothetical point at which AI surpasses human intelligence) and predictions that AI will take away all jobs. "All of that leads anyone who even wants to change to be sort of anxious … You have to sort of walk the hard walk of really making the structural changes, getting people slotted, giving them opportunity." In other words, the buyout was the message to employees: You can get with the new AI-first program, which will radically change your job, or you choose to get on with your life. Elsewhere. title: Microsoft publishes Aion, the small open model it plans to build into Windows by January - MLQ.ai
content: Microsoft has published Aion 1.0 Instruct, the small language model it plans to build into Windows, as an open model on Hugging Face [1]. The 2.3 billion parameter model comes from the Applied Sciences Group in Microsoft's Windows and Devices division and is released under the permissive MIT license [1]. The repository was created on Wednesday, Nov. 18 [2]. According to the model card, a further optimized version of Aion, coupled with Microsoft's content moderation model, will become the Windows OS small language model by the end of January 2027 [1]. Microsoft calls the Hugging Face release "an introduction to what's coming and a way to maximize transparency with our users" and says quantized versions will follow the unquantized weights [1]. Aion is meant for on-device text work: document comprehension, summarization, rewriting, question answering and chat, without a constant cloud connection [1]. Its 32,768-token context lets it read multi-page documents and long email threads on the device, which Microsoft pitches as keeping user data private [1]. It succeeds Phi Silica, the previous Windows OS model, and its training data is an extension of Phi Silica's: quality-filtered public documents plus synthetic data for math, coding and reasoning, with multilingual data about 6% of the total [1]. Its knowledge cutoff is December 2025 [1]. Technically it is a 28-layer transformer with about 2.29 billion parameters, a 200,029-token vocabulary and a hybrid attention design of 21 sliding-window layers and seven full-attention layers [1]. It runs with Hugging Face Transformers using custom code, and Microsoft also lists ONNX and GGUF formats; a separate ONNX build for WebGPU is on Hugging Face [1][3]. Microsoft ran the scores itself, mostly with EleutherAI's lm-evaluation-harness and GPT-4o as judge where one was needed [1]: The card is frank about limits. It says a model this size can miss details, make misstatements and struggle with multi-step reasoning, "may be susceptible to adversarial attacks," and lists cross-prompt injection (XPIA) among the safety metrics to improve in future releases [1]. That matters as Windows adds AI agents that act on users' behalf; a local content moderation model will run alongside Aion when it ships in Windows [1]. Azure is Microsoft's cloud computing platform and the main channel through which businesses access its AI services. Azure revenue grew at a rapid double-digit pace, accelerating from the prior quarter and topping forecasts. This happened even though some third-party providers delayed delivering data center capacity. For the first time, Microsoft disclosed Azure revenue as an exact dollar figure, giving investors clearer insight into the business. Microsoft moved from three reporting segments to two: Agents and Infra, and Devices and Consumer. The first includes Azure, its cloud productivity software and other business software. The Zhitong Finance APP learned that Morgan Stanley released a research report, reiterating its "Overweight" rating on Microsoft (MSFT.US) with a price target of $650. The Morgan Stanley analyst team led by Adam Wood stated that after Microsoft held its Ignite conference in San Francisco and interacted with CEO Nadella and CFO Amy Hood, the firm believes Microsoft is one of the few software companies that have already realized returns on their AI investments. Computing Power Strategy: Avoid blindly maximizing long-term GPU contracts; maintain diversified computing power service offerings. In its report, Morgan Stanley noted that, in allocating computing resources, Microsoft's management treats GPUs as modular assets and refrains from blindly pursuing long-term GPU-as-a-Service (GPUaaS) contracts. Management stated that the company will proactively reserve computing capacity to serve its own first-party products, the Foundry platform, and external enterprise customers, rather than locking all resources into long-term agreements. From Microsoft's perspective, model labs are merely key clients and do not represent the entirety of its cloud business; maintaining elastic computing capacity is a proactive investment in the value of its own platforms and applications, aimed at capturing monetization opportunities for high-value-added services built on top of its infrastructure. Regarding the market's attention to the Neocloud architecture strategy, Microsoft stated that its underlying strategy has not changed; the priority remains building its own data centers, followed by a long-term leasing model in which Microsoft controls data center fit-out, networking, and hardware equipment. This approach allows for better management of data center operational efficiency, deployment pace, and capital expenditures on equipment. The cancellation of some third-party partnership orders stems from suppliers' inadequate service performance, rather than a shift in Microsoft's overall computing power procurement strategy, nor does it signify a major change in the market's computing power supply-and-demand dynamics. Meanwhile, Microsoft's improvements in computing efficiency are not limited to the GPU level; CPU utilization and the storage system are also key focuses of optimization. Moreover, the newly deployed infrastructure inherits this optimization strategy, so the efficiency gains are not confined to existing server clusters. However, the bank cautions that efficiency gains should not be treated as an independent upward variable in computing capacity planning; rather, efficiency improvements can simultaneously boost revenue-carrying capacity and reduce delivery costs. Profitability and Gross Margin: Improvements at the product level take precedence, while the cloud business mix will temporarily weigh on the overall gross margin. Morgan Stanley specifically pointed out a key point that is easily confused by the market: Microsoft's management team's core objective is to improve the gross margins of Azure and M365 individually; the overall gross margin for Microsoft Cloud disclosed in the financial report is merely a result of business development, not a direct performance metric for management. Even if the profitability of individual products continues to improve, once the proportion of the high-growth but relatively low-margin Azure business keeps expanding, it will still dilute Microsoft's cloud consolidated gross margin. Investors should not simply conclude that the profitability of individual cloud services is weakening just because the overall gross margin is under pressure. When assessing future profit improvements, the focus should be on tracking resource utilization, infrastructure efficiency, model operating costs, and the consumption scale of high-value platform services. Enterprise AI Flywheel: Positioned as a multi-model orchestration layer, it is not limited to in-house large models; Microsoft IQ closes the capability loop. Microsoft does not bet its competitiveness on a single model; the core value for enterprise customers lies in the entire ecosystem surrounding the model: enterprise business context, model scheduling framework, memory capabilities, and secure, trustworthy governance. Enterprises can mix cutting-edge large models, Microsoft's self-developed specialized MAI models, and open-source weight models. The Microsoft platform is responsible for selecting the most cost-effective model based on task requirements to get the job done, while keeping control of enterprise business data with the customer and providing unified management of the security, permissions, and cost expenditures of all AI agents. At this conference, Microsoft IQ was unveiled, integrating Work IQ, Fabric IQ, Foundry IQ, and Web IQ, further connecting the entire enterprise AI flywheel and tightly coupling business data, model orchestration, and application distribution. Morgan Stanley believes that the more models available on the market, the higher the strategic value of Microsoft as a platform layer that bridges models and enterprise business workflows. Copilot Commercialization: Dual-Drive Model of Subscriptions and Pay-as-You-Go, with Early Adoption in Non-Code Scenarios Microsoft has adopted a hybrid business model that combines subscription-based pricing with usage-based billing: subscriptions provide stable base revenue, while usage-based billing generates incremental income in line with customers' actual AI workloads. Management disclosed that some large customers have already spent more on the Copilot Cowork product than on Microsoft's other products combined; however, the CFO team emphasized that this case is an extreme outlier and not representative of the broader customer base. Moreover, the product suite has only recently been commercialized, so it is still too early to establish reliable expectations for adoption rates. Currently, Copilot's adoption in coding-related workflows is strong, but consumer use across broader knowledge‑work scenarios remains in the early stages of development. While growth potential is significant, the pace of real‑world deployment remains a key uncertainty. Drawing an analogy to Azure's early development, management notes that as enterprises embrace AI agents, their demand for cost control and transparent spending is particularly pronounced. Microsoft has launched Agent 365, a business analytics and cost-management tool that ties AI expenditures to operational outcomes and budgetary alerts, helping companies manage fluctuating AI usage and remove barriers to large-scale deployment. However, the direct revenue generated by this suite of tools depends on the pace at which enterprises expand production-grade AI workloads. In-house chip strategy: Maia and Cobalt serve as efficiency supplements; not all workloads are migrated to in-house hardware. Microsoft's custom chips are part of a diversified computing fleet and do not aim to migrate all workloads to in-house hardware. Take the Maia AI chip and the newly released Cobalt 200 as examples: the Cobalt 200 targets agent-based AI workloads, delivering up to 50% better performance than its predecessor, the Cobalt 100. Microsoft will continue to procure chips from external vendors; the goal of its in-house chips is to enhance performance and reduce costs in specific scenarios, serving as a complementary lever for overall computing efficiency rather than an exclusive replacement. This approach continues the earlier trend of diversifying computing chips from a single source—Intel (INTC.US)—to include AMD (AMD.US) and Cobalt. title: House China committee asks Microsoft for a briefing on its reported AI cloud talks with ByteDance - MLQ.ai
content: The House select committee on China has asked Microsoft to brief lawmakers on reported talks to sell AI cloud services to ByteDance, committee Chairman John Moolenaar said on Wednesday, Nov. 18, Reuters reported [1]. "Microsoft should not sell AI tools to ByteDance," Moolenaar, a Michigan Republican, said in a statement. "Leading American technology companies should not be playing both sides of the U.S-China AI race" [1]. The request follows a report by The Information that ByteDance is in advanced talks to spend roughly $500 million more on Microsoft cloud services, mainly to use OpenAI models through Azure, citing two people with knowledge of the situation [3]. OpenAI blocks most Chinese companies from using its AI directly, but Microsoft holds rights to resell the technology and does not face the same restriction, according to the report [3]. OpenAI has told Microsoft in recent months that it believes Chinese firms are running its models to build competing ones, the report said [3]. The committee's website listed no letter or statement on the matter at about 4:45 p.m. ET, so the signatories, any deadline and the specific questions are not public [2]. The Reuters report did not include a response from Microsoft [1]. Neither Microsoft nor ByteDance has publicly confirmed the reported talks in the sources reviewed by MLQ.ai. title: Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) Patched A Record 1,400 Security Flaws In A Single Month As A "Vullpocalypse" Grips Critical Digital Infrastructure - Foreign Policy Journal
content: By Ewan Scott | Nov 18, 2026 | Economy & Business, Featured, News & Analysis A staggering jump in software vulnerability fixes is reframing how analysts and everyday users understand the wave of technology disruptions hitting major institutions. Microsoft (NASDAQ: MSFT) issued patches addressing roughly 1,400 security flaws during a single monthly update, a figure that dwarfs the 170 fixes recorded in the same period a year earlier. The Wall Street Journal reported the record-breaking numbers, which analysts on Yahoo Finance’s “The 8:30” cited as a key data point in understanding the current disruption environment. The outages have touched a broad range of institutions, including Apple (NASDAQ: AAPL), JPMorgan Chase (NYSE: JPM), and the National Security Agency, alongside Microsoft itself. Hosts Julie Hyman, Pras Subramanian, and Jake Conley discussed how artificial intelligence is now surfacing software exploits at a pace that far outstrips traditional patching cycles, forcing developers to push fixes faster than systems can absorb them. The theory gaining traction among technology professionals is that decades of layered software, built upon older code that engineers no longer fully understand, is fracturing under the pressure of rapid remediation efforts. The phenomenon has been informally dubbed a “Vullpocalypse,” a portmanteau of “vulnerability” and “apocalypse,” capturing the sheer scale of simultaneous security fixes cascading through interconnected systems. Secretary of State Marco Rubio, questioned about the outages while in the Philippines ahead of the Trilateral Summit, pushed back firmly against any suggestion of a coordinated attack or systemic link between the incidents. Rubio stated, “The Microsoft incident has nothing to do with what we saw with the FAA. The FAA has nothing to do with what we saw with the banks a few days ago. These issues that we’ve seen from a technical standpoint are completely unrelated from one another,” adding there was “zero evidence that everything’s connected.” Beyond the technical debate, panelist Jake Conley identified a growing sentiment problem, noting that disruptions are no longer abstract concerns confined to cybersecurity professionals. When ordinary consumers cannot access their bank accounts or face repeated software update prompts across their devices, public anxiety rises in ways that governments and technology companies will be forced to address. The broader backdrop, as Conley observed, is that society is now more deeply embedded in these digital systems than at any previous point, meaning the consequences of instability ripple further and faster than ever before. Ewan is a reporter at the Foreign Policy Journal, primarily covering US current affairs and news related to NYSE-listed stocks. He has over two decades of experience in journalism and digital publishing.

title: Microsoft (MSFT) Stock: New AI Model Takes Aim at Anthropic and OpenAI on Price - Blockonomi
content: Microsoft (MSFT) is trying to win on price, not just power. At its Ignite conference in San Francisco on Tuesday, the company showed off a batch of new AI models. The star is MAI Code 2, a computer programming model. Microsoft says it almost matches rival models on performance at a fraction of the cost. The rivals in question are Anthropic and OpenAI. Microsoft is racing to challenge both. MICROSOFT ANNOUNCES 6 NEW AI MODELS AT IGNITE$MSFT unveiled six MAI models across coding, cybersecurity, image generation and voice on the same day its partner OpenAI released GPT-6.2. 1) MAI Code 2: Delivers 98% of GPT-6.1 Sol's performance at 40% of the cost. Now in GitHub… pic.twitter.com/yn6qA2K17c Coding was not the only launch. Microsoft also unveiled a model built just for cybersecurity. Most customers will not get it right away. The company plans to offer it to a limited group. The goal is to deal with a surge in software vulnerabilities. AI tools are increasingly bringing those flaws to light. Microsoft also released new image-generation and transcription models. That makes four model launches in a single event. AI chief Mustafa Suleyman says the trick is going narrow. Building technology for specific domains keeps costs low, he told Reuters. He says that approach lets Microsoft match rivals and, in some cases, top model benchmarks. The company is not leaning on one giant model to do it. “This isn’t just one model. It’s not a flash in the pan,” he said. He called it “a system, a hill-climbing machine” that co-optimizes performance and price. Think of it as a toolbox instead of one giant hammer. Each model gets a job and a budget. Suleyman said the recent cybersecurity reckoning changed his focus. He pointed to OpenAI agents hacking the Hugging Face platform. He now looks at safeguards as well as performance. Alignment is his top priority. Alignment is the research area aimed at stopping AI from taking harmful actions. It also means making sure the AI behaves as intended. Ignite also brought news on outside models. CEO Satya Nadella said Meta’s latest AI models are coming to Microsoft Foundry. Foundry is Microsoft’s platform for building AI applications and agents on Azure.
